name: Half Guard to Leg Weave
description: Entering Leg Weave from half guard threads an arm through the leg gap to control the lower thigh or knee and fold the knee shield toward the other leg.
aliases: Knee Weave Entry from Half Guard
summary: Entering Leg Weave from half guard threads an arm through the leg gap to control the lower thigh or knee and fold the knee shield toward the other leg.
overview:
The top passer begins in Half Guard, facing a knee shield or linked leg frame. The weaving limb is the arm. Securing that control is the entry checkpoint; a pass is complete only after the hips and remaining leg hooks are cleared.

Thread the arm through the available leg gap and connect to the lower thigh or knee. Use aligned shoulder pressure and chest pressure to bring the knees together without twisting the knee joint. Avoid leaving the weaving arm extended where the bottom player can sit up into a kimura.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Lachlan Giles — leg weave pass, no gi](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9rDzchSk4fw); [Lachlan Giles — leg-weave counter demonstration](https://bjjfanatics.com/blogs/news/interesting-leg-weave-counter-with-lachlan-giles).

attacker.name: Half Guard to Leg Weave Attacker
attacker.description: Half Guard to Leg Weave (attacker): Thread the arm through the available leg gap and connect to the lower thigh or knee. Use aligned shoulder pressure and chest pressure to bring the knees together without twisting the knee joint.
attacker.overview:
The top passer begins in Half Guard, facing a knee shield or linked leg frame. The weaving limb is the arm. Securing that control is the entry checkpoint; a pass is complete only after the hips and remaining leg hooks are cleared.

Thread the arm through the available leg gap and connect to the lower thigh or knee. Use aligned shoulder pressure and chest pressure to bring the knees together without twisting the knee joint. Avoid leaving the weaving arm extended where the bottom player can sit up into a kimura.

Move the hips and feet without collapsing all weight over the woven arm. Remove the remaining foot or half-guard hook before establishing side control. If the bottom player turns or inserts a frame, keep control of distance and reset the pass rather than forcing a fixed angle.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Pair the weaving arm with head position and control of the opposing elbow. This hip control limits the knees following as you start to circle; reaching for a crossface before the weave is stable gives up the head-and-arm position needed to keep the shield folded.

Manage the knee shield: Use aligned shoulder pressure and chest pressure to bring the knees together without twisting the knee joint.

Maintain an outside base: Move the hips and feet without collapsing all weight over the woven arm.
Clear the legs before settling: Remove the remaining foot or half-guard hook before establishing side control.
Follow the hips: If the bottom player turns or inserts a frame, keep control of distance and reset the pass rather than forcing a fixed angle.

defender.name: Half Guard to Leg Weave Defender
defender.description: Half Guard to Leg Weave (defender): The passer's arm connecting your legs is the relevant control, not a leg threaded across your hip. Maintain a useful knee angle and upper-body frame before the passer folds the legs together.
defender.overview:
The top passer begins in Half Guard, facing a knee shield or linked leg frame. The weaving limb is the arm. Securing that control is the entry checkpoint; a pass is complete only after the hips and remaining leg hooks are cleared.

The passer's arm connecting your legs is the relevant control, not a leg threaded across your hip. Maintain a useful knee angle and upper-body frame before the passer folds the legs together. Move the hips and pummel the knee back between the bodies while the weave is still loose.

Prevent the passer from flattening your shoulders while controlling the legs. An underhook can help you face the passer and rebuild half guard when the shoulder line is not already pinned. Do not wrench a knee out of a fixed weave; create room with the hips and frames first.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Use hip movement and the upper-body frame to recover an inside knee while the arm weave remains loose. Move the whole leg with the hips instead of twisting a knee held between the passer's grips.

Frame across the passer's shoulder line to turn the head away while keeping the knee shield supported. A short shrimp creates room for the knee to return as an early escape; if you sit up to an underhook, expect an overhook response and maintain the base needed to face it.
key_principles: Recognize the arm weave: The passer's arm connecting your legs is the relevant control, not a leg threaded across your hip.
Keep the shield supported: Maintain a useful knee angle and upper-body frame before the passer folds the legs together.
Recover inside space: Move the hips and pummel the knee back between the bodies while the weave is still loose.
Deny upper-body collapse: Prevent the passer from flattening your shoulders while controlling the legs.
Use an available underhook: An underhook can help you face the passer and rebuild half guard when the shoulder line is not already pinned.
Move the whole leg: Do not wrench a knee out of a fixed weave; create room with the hips and frames first.
